subject: science
title: KS3 / Year 7-9 Science — Chemistry: Particles Reading
subtitle: Reading comprehension on the particle model, states, changes of state, diffusion and investigations.
description: A source-faithful reading pack for KS3 chemistry. Passages test explanation, evidence and application of particle ideas in diagrams, changes of state, diffusion, graphs and practical work.

data.sourcePassage: The particle model says that all matter is made from tiny particles. Matter means anything that has mass and takes up space, so air, water, metal, wood, smoke and skin are all matter. Individual particles are much too small to see with a school microscope, so scientists use a model to explain what substances do. A particle diagram usually shows particles as circles. It can show whether they are close together or far apart, and whether they are arranged regularly or randomly. However, it is not an exact picture. It does not show the true size, shape or number of particles in a real sample. A good explanation uses the model carefully and links observations to particle arrangement, movement and energy.

questions.question: What does matter mean?
questions.modelAnswer: Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space.

questions.question: Why do scientists use the particle model in KS3 science?
options: Because individual particles are too small to see with a school microscope
Because particles are always visible in normal lessons
Because models are exact photographs of matter
Because matter does not have mass
questions.modelAnswer: Scientists use the particle model because individual particles are too small to see with a school microscope.

questions.question: Give two things a particle diagram can show.
questions.modelAnswer: It can show whether particles are close together or far apart, and whether they are in a regular or random arrangement.

questions.question: Why is it important to say that a particle diagram is a model, not an exact picture?
questions.modelAnswer: It is important because the diagram simplifies reality. It does not show the true size, shape, number or exact distance between particles in a real sample.

questions.question: What three particle ideas should a strong explanation link to?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong explanation should link to particle arrangement, movement and energy.

data.sourcePassage: Solids, liquids and gases behave differently because their particles are arranged and move differently. In a solid, particles are close together and held in fixed positions. They only vibrate, so a solid keeps a fixed shape and a fixed volume. In a liquid, particles are close together but arranged randomly. They can move and slide past each other, so a liquid flows and takes the shape of its container. It still has a fixed volume because the particles are close together. In a gas, particles are far apart and move quickly in all directions. A gas fills its container and is easy to compress because there is lots of empty space between particles. The particles themselves do not shrink during compression.

questions.question: Which statement best describes particles in a solid?
options: They are far apart and move quickly in all directions
They are close together and vibrate around fixed positions
They are close together but move freely to fill any container
They are far apart in a regular pattern
questions.modelAnswer: Solid particles are close together and vibrate around fixed positions.

questions.question: Why does a liquid flow?
questions.modelAnswer: A liquid flows because its particles can move and slide past each other.

questions.question: Explain why a gas can be compressed but a liquid is difficult to compress.
questions.modelAnswer: A gas has particles far apart with lots of empty space between them, so they can be pushed closer together. Liquid particles are already close together, so there is little empty space.

questions.question: A student says, 'A liquid takes the shape of a beaker because it is wet.' Improve this using particle ideas.
questions.modelAnswer: A liquid takes the shape of a beaker because its particles are close together but can move and slide past each other.

questions.question: What happens to gas particles themselves during compression?
questions.modelAnswer: The particles are pushed closer together, but the particles themselves do not shrink.

data.sourceTitle: Heating, Cooling and Changes of State
data.targetTitle: Heating, Cooling and Changes of State
data.sourcePassage: Heating transfers energy to particles. When particles gain energy, they move or vibrate more. Cooling removes energy, so particles move or vibrate less. During melting, a solid is heated until its particles have enough energy to overcome some forces holding them in fixed positions. The particles remain close together, but they can move around each other, so the substance becomes a liquid. During freezing, energy is removed from a liquid and particles become held in fixed positions. Boiling is liquid changing to gas throughout the liquid at its boiling point. Evaporation is different because it happens only from the surface and can happen below the boiling point. Condensation happens when gas particles lose energy, slow down and come closer together to form a liquid.

questions.question: What happens to particles when they are heated?
questions.modelAnswer: They gain energy and move or vibrate more.

questions.question: Which change of state is liquid to gas from the surface below boiling point?
options: Condensation
Freezing
Evaporation
Melting
questions.modelAnswer: Evaporation is liquid changing to gas from the surface below boiling point.

questions.question: Explain melting using particle movement and forces of attraction.
questions.modelAnswer: When a solid is heated, particles gain energy and vibrate more strongly. At the melting point they overcome some forces of attraction, so they can move around each other as a liquid.

questions.question: Give two differences between boiling and evaporation.
questions.modelAnswer: Boiling happens throughout the liquid and at the boiling point. Evaporation happens at the surface only and can happen below the boiling point.

questions.question: Why does condensation form droplets on a cold mirror after a shower?
questions.modelAnswer: Water vapour particles touch the cooler mirror, lose energy, move more slowly and are pulled closer together into liquid droplets.

data.sourcePassage: A heating curve shows how temperature changes as a substance is heated. Sloping sections show temperature increasing while the substance warms in one state. Flat sections show a change of state. During a flat section, energy is still being transferred, but the temperature does not rise because the energy is used to overcome forces of attraction between particles. The melting point can be read from the flat section where solid changes to liquid. The boiling point can be read from the flat section where liquid changes to gas. On a cooling curve, sloping sections show temperature decreasing. Flat sections show freezing or condensation, where energy is transferred from the substance to the surroundings while the arrangement of particles changes.

questions.question: What does a sloping section on a heating curve show?
options: Temperature increasing while the substance warms in one state
Particles disappearing
The substance cooling down
No energy being transferred
questions.modelAnswer: A sloping section shows temperature increasing while the substance warms in one state.

questions.question: What does a flat section on a heating curve usually show?
questions.modelAnswer: It shows that a change of state is happening.

questions.question: Why does temperature not rise during a flat section on a heating curve?
questions.modelAnswer: Energy is still transferred, but it is used to overcome forces of attraction between particles rather than increasing the temperature.

questions.question: How can the melting point be found from a heating curve?
questions.modelAnswer: It is read from the flat section where the solid changes to a liquid.

questions.question: What is different about the direction of energy transfer on a cooling curve compared with a heating curve?
questions.modelAnswer: On a cooling curve, energy is transferred from the substance to the surroundings. On a heating curve, energy is transferred to the substance.

data.sourcePassage: Diffusion is the spreading out of particles from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration. It happens because particles move randomly. In a KS3 investigation, a student can test how temperature affects the rate of diffusion of food colouring in water. The independent variable is the temperature of the water. The dependent variable is the time taken for the colour to spread evenly. Control variables include the volume of water, size of beaker, amount of food colouring, starting position of the drop and whether the water is stirred. The prediction is that food colouring will diffuse faster in warmer water because particles have more energy and move faster. Reliability is improved by repeating each test and calculating a mean time.

questions.question: Define diffusion.
questions.modelAnswer: Diffusion is the spreading of particles from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration.

questions.question: In this investigation, what is the independent variable?
options: Temperature of the water
Time taken for colour to spread evenly
The colour of the beaker
The mean time
questions.modelAnswer: The independent variable is the temperature of the water.

questions.question: What is the dependent variable in the food colouring investigation?
questions.modelAnswer: It is the time taken for the colour to spread evenly through the water.

questions.question: Explain why diffusion is expected to be faster in warmer water.
questions.modelAnswer: Particles in warmer water have more energy and move faster, so the food colouring particles spread out more quickly.

questions.question: Give two control variables for this investigation.
questions.modelAnswer: Valid examples include volume of water, size of beaker, amount of food colouring, starting position of the drop, colour used or whether the water is stirred.

questions.question: Why does repeating the test and calculating a mean improve the investigation?
questions.modelAnswer: It improves reliability because repeated results show whether the measurements are consistent, and a mean reduces the effect of unusual results.
